lockedMove.speaker: Erik Wielenberg
lockedMove.proposition: Godless normative realism can accommodate supererogatory action through exclusionary permissions, while Christian love commands may render the proposed theistic examples obligatory.
lockedMove.sourceExcerpt: examples of sacrificing your life for others and becoming a doctor rather than an engineer. I have two thoughts here. First, I'm not convinced that Craig's view allows such acts to be above and beyond what is morally obligatory. Although Craig spoke only of generic theism in his opening speech, his view is a version of Christian theism, according to which one of God's central commands to us is to love

components.text: The decisive demand is whether the reasons-based account can permit genuinely supererogatory conduct rather than requiring every morally best act.
A second demand is whether decisive moral reasons generate unconditional rather than merely desire-dependent obligations.

response.rationale: The reply contacts supererogation through exclusionary permissions and challenges whether Craig's Christian commands preserve his examples, but it does not answer the conditional-duty objection.
